item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers clinched a postseason spot for the 14th consecutive season and are closing in on a 13th National League West title during that span.
Also of importance for the Dodgers is finishing with a top two record in the NL as it would come with a first-round bye in the playoffs. That could be of particular value to a slew of injured Dodgers, including Shohei Ohtani, Andy Pages, Dalton Rushing and Edgardo Henriquez.
Dodgers updates
Dalton Rushing
Rushing made a surprising return on Sept. 1 from a slight tear in the UCL of his right elbow, but only managed to appear in four games off the bench before going back on the 10-day injured list. That came after Rushing was scratched from the lineup due to right elbow trouble that stemmed from his attempt at a throwing progression.
The Dodgers have since ruled out Rushing possibly catching again this year, but they remain hopeful he will be an option as a left-handed bat off the bench.
“Dalton’s doing well,” manager Dave Roberts said on SportsNet LA. “Building up his progression.”
Shohei Ohtani
Ohtani started his swinging progression on Tuesday by hitting off a tee. Roberts said he “felt good” doing so and is going to continue moving along.
“I don’t know what’s in store for tomorrow, but I know there’s going to be a consistent buildup. Don’t know when the time to return to play is, but today was positive and hopefully we can just keep building toward that,” Roberts said.
Roberts added he believes Ohtani will return at some point in the regular season, but cautioned, “Whether it happens or not is to be determined.”
Ohtani is eligible to be activated off the 15-day injured list Sept. 23.
Andy Pages
Pages has been swinging a bat for several days and took a step forward on Tuesday by hitting off pitching machine. Next for Pages is to log at-bats against the Trajekt machine.
Edgardo Henriquez
Henriquez, the latest Dodgers injury, returned to Los Angeles in order to undergo testing on his back/side area. He was officially put on the 15-day injured list due to low back discomfort, but Roberts noted there might be some trouble with the oblique as well.
Henriquez is not eligible to return during the regular season but the Dodgers hope he will be available for the playoffs.
Have you subscribed to the Dodger Blue YouTube channel? Be sure to ring the notification bell to watch player interviews, participate in shows and giveaways, and stay up to date on all Dodgers news and rumors!

item.content:encoded:
The other day I walked outside my apartment in New York and noticed the slightest hint of a chill in the morning air. And I could only think of one thing: the postseason is almost here. The long baseball season is drawing to a close. The delight of October awaits.
And then …
Oh, yeah. The lockout.
The next few months could reshape the future of baseball. I suppose we shall see how it goes. Until then, let’s take some questions. As always, they have been edited for clarity.
Advertisement
Which wild-card team has the best chance to upset a division winner? — bbrathizza2075
There are a lot of worthy candidates, especially in the National League. But I would have to say the Yankees, if only because on paper, the Yankees should be the best team in the American League, even if they are unlikely to catch the American League East. The Yankees lead the AL in run differential by a significant margin. No AL lineup has hit more home runs. In Cam Schlittler, they employ the Cy Young favorite. And they still have Aaron Judge.
So the Yankees would be my pick, but the talent on the other wild-card clubs is immense. The Phillies can line up Cristopher Sánchez, Zack Wheeler and, if he’s healthy, Jesús Luzardo in a five-game series. Good luck. Pete Crow-Armstrong has been the best player in baseball for a Cubs team that boasts the best offense in baseball. A healthy Nick Pivetta provides San Diego with enough rotation stability for a short series, in which their bullpen would be hellish to face. And the Padres, who would likely face the Dodgers, have shown a willingness in recent years to stand and trade blows with baseball’s reigning champs.
And, really, what qualifies as an upset? If the 98-win Rays lose to the 94-win Yankees in a five-game series, would it really be shocking? Same story with the Phillies or the Cubs facing the Brewers. These teams will be quite evenly matched. It should be an entertaining October.
Which National League fanbase would be MOST disappointed if its team doesn’t hoist the commissioner’s trophy in 2026? Big narrative-ball postseason for Brewers, Phillies and even Cubs fans in my opinion. — Jacob N.
I think it’s a toss-up between Milwaukee and Philadelphia. And I would lean toward the Phillies.
When it comes to the Brewers, a lot of folks in baseball have asked the question: If not now, when? Well, the team made clear, in part by declining to go bonkers and acquire Tarik Skubal, that it rejects the premise. And the Brewers brain trust may be wise to do so. This team is well-situated to contend in 2026, but also well beyond 2026. Jackson Chourio is 22. Jacob Misiorowski is 24. Logan Henderson is 24. Brice Turang is practically ancient at 26. Jesús Made and Luis Peña are on the way. This team isn’t going anywhere.
Right. Right?
Well …
Baltimore fans felt the same way after a 101-win campaign in 2023. Instead, they’ve watched the Orioles degrade from budding juggernaut into a last-place club. And while I do not foresee that fate for the Brewers, it remains within the realm of possibility. Misiorowski may not stay healthy beyond this season. The 2026 campaign could be this group’s best chance to win the first championship in franchise history.
Advertisement
Even so, I don’t think the psychological blow of an early exit would sting Brewers fans like it would Phillies fans. There is just so much frustration stored up within that fanbase, dating to that shocking collapse in the 2023 National League Championship Series. There are also legitimate questions about how long the window will remain open for this group. Again, it comes back to age. Kyle Schwarber is 33. Bryce Harper turns 34 in October. Zack Wheeler is 36. Trea Turner is playing below-replacement-level at 33 — and his contract will not expire until 2033. The farm system has not produced much in recent years, and Dave Dombrowski has not done well on the free-agent market.
So while Brewers fans may be infuriated about the unfairness of MLB’s system, and while they may lament another missed opportunity, they can credibly believe they will have another shot in 2027. That is harder to fathom for Phillies fans.
The first two teams to clinch playoff berths were the Rays and Brewers. Could you shed any light on the Tampa Bay model both teams adhere to? — Gary D.
Back in 2021, I wrote a lengthy feature about the Rays and their ruthless roster building. The simplest way to describe it is they make a lot of transactions, and that churning allows them to occasionally unearth stars.
Here is one example. Back in 2008, the Rays chose Tim Beckham with the first overall pick in the draft. Beckham was essentially a bust. He took five years to reach the majors and never really hit. In 2017, after nearly a decade of trying to develop him, Tampa Bay dealt Beckham to Baltimore for minor-league pitcher Tobias Myers. He spent a few seasons in Tampa Bay’s farm system before getting traded to Cleveland for a teenage prospect from the Dominican Republic. You may have heard of him by now: Junior Caminero. And Caminero has become the sort of star the Rays once envisioned Beckham could have been. The team turned a failure into a smashing success.
Now, most front offices don’t get a decade to oversee decisions like this. Andrew Friedman was in charge when Beckham was drafted. Chaim Bloom was running the show when Beckham was traded. And Erik Neander, who has worked in the organization since 2007, was the head of baseball operations for the Caminero deal. But the organizational ethos hasn’t changed all that much over the past decade.
Advertisement
Milwaukee also tends toward roster churn but is a tad less aggressive than Tampa Bay. The Brewers are run by Rays alum Matt Arnold, and that man does love a three-team trade. They can find great production on the margins, as they have this season with Jake Bauers. And they are unafraid to deal star players as their contracts expire, as they did in recent years with Corbin Burnes, Devin Williams and Freddy Peralta. Where Milwaukee really excels is scouting Latin America. It signed Chourio and outfielder Luis Lara out of Venezuela. They signed Made and Peña out of the Dominican.
These are the things that small-market teams would like to emulate. Do well in the draft. Don’t stay static on the margins of the roster. And excel in finding stars out of the international market. If it was easy, every team would do it.
Do you think we have seen the last of Shohei Ohtani as a pitcher/starter? — Tae K.
I do not. He will pitch again. But how the Dodgers deploy him will be fascinating.
Multiple things can be true:
1. Shohei Ohtani might be the best pitcher in the world.
He demonstrated that during his 14 starts this season. He posted a 1.79 ERA while striking out 10 batters per nine innings. And he did that while toting the responsibility of batting leadoff as the designated hitter most days in between outings. He looked, in a word, awesome.
2. As he enters his mid-30s, Ohtani probably cannot complete a full season as a two-way player.
The basic story of Ohtani’s professional life is people within baseball telling him, “Hey! You can’t do that,” and Ohtani responding, “Well, actually, I can.” But Father Time is undefeated, and Ohtani has learned that the two-way load is far tougher to shoulder at 32 than it was at 27. He is currently on the injured list dealing with problems with his neck, knee and biceps. And there may be other maladies the famously private Ohtani has not revealed. Suffice to say, he is quite banged up, and no one within the Dodgers organization is thrilled about the situation.
Advertisement
These two facts — Ohtani’s greatness and his fallibility — present the Dodgers with a conflict. There is a clear compromise: the team should ask him to spend the first half of the season as a hitter and then use the second half to build up arm strength so he can be available to pitch in October. Problem solved!
Well, not exactly. Ohtani has agency in this situation. He may not want to give up the full-season two-way dream so easily. He may still want to prove that he can do in his 30s what he did in his 20s. He may still want to say, “Well, actually, I can.” And the Dodgers may not want to scuffle with the face of the franchise. It will be a delicate dance.
How Ohtani feels about his future is unclear. He has not spoken to reporters since Sept. 7, and did not accompany the club on its current trip to Miami and Cincinnati. But he has been staunch his entire career about wanting to remain a two-way player. “The reason why I’m a two-way player is because that’s who I am,” he said during the 2025 postseason. “And it’s what I can do.”
I still think he can be a two-way player, and I would be shocked if he tried to only hit moving forward. But the prospect of him being a healthy two-way player over the course of a 162-game season feels more like a fantasy than a reality. Then again, Ohtani has shown us, over and over in his career, that he can make dreams come true.
Catchers were the overwhelming best at ABS challenges, but I am curious how they fared at challenging as batters compared to batters at other positions. — Anonymous
Interesting premise.
I looked this up and found essentially no correlation. Now, there may be a connection, because while I am not a math wizard, I don’t think one unfinished season provides enough data for a sufficient sample size. At least this year, there is little evidence that, as hitters, catchers perform better than other hitters with ABS.
Dillon Dingler entered Monday’s games rated as the best challenger among catchers, according to FanGraphs. But as a hitter? Dingler graded below average. Same story for Hunter Goodman and J.T. Realmuto, the two catchers rated best behind Dingler.
Among the hitters, there were two catchers rated in Savant’s top 10 for ABS efficiency: Tyler Stephenson and Gabriel Moreno. Iván Herrera came in at No. 14. But then no catcher appears on the leaderboard until Brandon Valenzuela at No. 34. So, like I said, interesting premise, but no real correlation that this knucklehead who flunked geometry in high school can find.
Advertisement
For the last couple of decades, Major League Baseball has seemed to have a major “household name” gap with the NBA and NFL, and Rob Manfred once addressed this by complaining that Mike Trout wasn’t doing more to make himself famous. How is the league working to grow its fanbase and promote its product? — Alex R.
The owners are planning to lock out the players when the collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1.
What are your most realistic thoughts on the lockout? — pollrobb
When I talk to people in baseball about the lockout, they usually say some version of the same thing: they really don’t know what will happen, but they think it will be bad. The negotiations will be contentious. The rhetoric will be vicious. They may well miss games.
My guess — and I will repeat that this is a guess — is that the lockout resolves at some point in March, with enough time to cram a 162-game season into the calendar, in a result similar to the last lockout. I do not foresee the players caving and accepting a salary cap. But it is also hard to identify, in that scenario, what would trigger the owners to stop pushing for one. Genuinely, I do not know how it will go, and anyone who tells you they do is probably overselling their insight.
Why would the players and league not work on solving 100 small things in negotiation now and figure out the big topic at the end? Is it really going to wreck what they have while fighting over billions of dollars? I truly enjoy the game and can’t believe they say it can all wait until December, so they can blame each other. Why not now? — Lynn Z.
To be fair, the two sides have traded a variety of proposals on issues besides the salary cap. They are negotiating. But the small stuff is small for a reason. And the big thing — the potential implementation of a salary cap — is much bigger than anything on the table in the previous round of negotiations. For the owners, the possibility of a cap means billions of dollars gained in franchise values. But for the players, accepting a cap means the collapse of the free-market system that the union has fought so strenuously to maintain for decades. These are existential questions for both sides. And neither side will be inclined to budge until the calendar flips into 2027 and spring training draws closer. So, buckle up. It is going to be a long, bumpy ride.

item.title: [The New York Times] ‘I just want to feel saucy’: Inside Josue De Paula’s fearless Dodgers debut

item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI — Josue De Paula is in his element in the batter’s box. He carries himself like a guy who knows his importance to the Los Angeles Dodgers depends on how well he can command himself within those 24 square feet of chalk lines. De Paula asserts himself with a confident shake of the head after each pitch outside the strike zone.
Advertisement
Some head shakes are more exaggerated than others. Each demonstrates the same message: De Paula is not going to give in.
“I just want to feel saucy when I’m up there, you know what I’m saying?” De Paula told The Athletic this week. “I feel like I’m in control, not you. … I want my pitch. Come in the zone. Let’s go.”
This is who De Paula wants to be. He describes hitting as “aggressive patience,” an approach that puts him on the attack.
“It’s almost like a war for me in my head,” De Paula said. “I look confident. I look saucy. I feel saucy when I’m in the box, so it’s like, ‘Hey bro, let’s keep it rocking.’”
It took four games for De Paula to inspire fascination within the Dodgers dynasty, where his every at-bat feels like a must-watch example of how to command a zone. Of the first 37 big-league pitches De Paula saw outside of the strike zone, he swung at just five. He made it 17 plate appearances without striking out before going down swinging in the seventh inning and looking in the ninth in the Dodgers’ 4-0 win over the Reds on Tuesday. De Paula does not seem fazed that he is just 2 for 14 (.143) since being called up, including five hitless at-bats in his first game in the leadoff spot.
That’s because he believes in his process. A day earlier, De Paula battled back from down in the count against Reds lefty Nick Lodolo, a former All-Star. The left-handed batter took a 2-2 fastball just below the knees, crouched and shook his head. A pitch later, De Paula walked for the fifth time in his short career.
The clip of the head shake drew a chuckle from the proprietor of the “Soto Shuffle” himself, Juan Soto, who, like De Paula, once honed his craft at the El Niche Baseball Academy in the Dominican city of Santo Domingo.
Josue De Paula live reaction to you trying to get him to chase. https://t.co/CrmRSnDVgO pic.twitter.com/dbXGz8WYL0
— Chad Moriyama (@ChadMoriyama) September 14, 2026
“El loco mío,” Soto shared to his Instagram story in Spanish, stamping his approval with a laughing emoji. My guy.
Advertisement
“I swear I wasn’t trying to do like the whole thing,” De Paula said with a laugh. “I just got into my legs, and I was shaking my head … but I’m not mad. That’s not a bad player to look like.”
De Paula, 21, feels like an injection of youthful exuberance for baseball’s oldest lineup. The Brooklyn-born son of a Dominican father (and relative of NBA veterans Stephon Marbury and Sebastian Telfair) speaks with a thick New York accent and oozes the confidence of a player who carries that swagger into the box.
De Paula is the crown jewel of a Dodgers farm system that is expected to prolong this run of excellence. Last week, he became the first position player ever to be called up directly from Double A by this Andrew Friedman-led front office group.
De Paula is here because he can hit, has always hit, and the Dodgers need him to hit. De Paula is here to serve as the Dodgers’ designated hitter, at least until Shohei Ohtani returns from the injured list. No one with the Dodgers, however, is ruling out the possibility that De Paula could help them in October as they seek a third consecutive World Series title.
“I hope he makes our decision hard,” manager Dave Roberts said.
Through De Paula’s torrid run through the Dodgers’ farm system, officials raved about his keen ability to pick up the baseball, make proper swing decisions and recognize spin.
“He doesn’t give away any pitches, which I love, let alone give away any at-bats,” Roberts said.
Pair that with a preternatural ability to make contact, and De Paula entered this season as one of the highly-regarded young hitters in the league. The Dodgers implemented a change to De Paula’s swing this year, lowering his hands and opening up his resulting bat path to keep the barrel in the zone longer. That has allowed him to access more power by pulling more fly balls and has made him a lethal producer at Double A.
Advertisement
De Paula slugged 27 home runs this season in Double A, more than double what he had in any of his first four professional seasons. His first hit Sunday in Miami was a mammoth upper-deck shot to right field on the kind of awe-inspiring swing that has come much more easily for De Paula than in years past.
“When all those things are kind of clicking, it’s tough for any pitcher to compete with,” hitting coach Robert Van Scoyoc said. “So it’s been very impressive so far.”
De Paula became a Dodger partially as a byproduct of the COVID-19 pandemic, which shut down the New York baseball season and prompted De Paula’s father, Josue Sr., to send him to the Dominican Republic to work at El Niche under Cristian “Niche” Batista.
“It was like stepping into a whole other world,” De Paula said.
It was there, during an offseason workout, that De Paula met Soto, who broke into the big leagues at 19 years old with the kind of swaggering command of the batter’s box that De Paula hopes to replicate. Rather than enter the amateur draft, De Paula signed directly with the Dodgers as an international amateur for a bonus of just under $400,000. De Paula estimated that, in one of his two tryouts with the organization and with several of the club’s brass in attendance, he collected nine hits in 10 at-bats.
“I killed,” De Paula said, reliving the memory as if it just happened.
He has hit ever since, ascending to the top of prospect lists. His list of star-studded admirers grew, too. After accompanying Soto in being represented by super agent Scott Boras, De Paula was asked by Boras to name some of his favorite players. De Paula selected Elly De La Cruz, who at that time was set for his first season as a breakout star for the Cincinnati Reds but was already dominating the minor leagues. Boras invited De Paula to his Newport Beach offices in Southern California after that and surprised him by bringing De La Cruz.
Advertisement
The two have remained close, working out together in the Miami area in the winters. Friday, just before he made his major-league debut against the Marlins in Miami, De Paula called De La Cruz on FaceTime. When they met up again this week in Cincinnati, they posed for a picture.
“I’m really happy for what he’s doing,” De La Cruz said.
De Paula sees a kinship between De La Cruz and Soto.
“We’re all killers,” De Paula said with a knowing smirk.
When De Paula spent his first spring training in big-league camp with the Dodgers in 2025, he quickly heard from Mookie Betts. The former Gold Glove right fielder wanted to make De Paula and fellow newcomers Zyhir Hope and Justin Dean feel welcome, so over dinner at a Phoenix-area soul food restaurant, he talked shop. When De Paula went out for early defensive work in the outfield this week, he had Roberts and Betts at different points offer some advice.
Now in a clubhouse filled with stars, De Paula said he feels at home. Whether he stays there heading into October will depend on how the rest of the regular season goes. The first few games have left a strong first impression.
“It’s a slow heartbeat,” Van Scoyoc said. “He’s not overwhelmed at all. It seemed like he picked up where he left off in Double A. … I wouldn’t say it’s surprising, but it’s just nice to see.”
Ohtani is expected to return from his nagging biceps and knee injuries by year’s end. De Paula has a lack of defensive utility at this point. While he did play in left field on Sunday, the Dodgers still want to work on getting De Paula to “value” the defensive side of the ball first, Roberts said. That means his path to the Dodgers’ postseason roster will likely be as a left-handed bat off the bench, essentially the role the club envisioned for Dalton Rushing before his most recent IL stint.
Advertisement
That decision is still up in the air, Roberts said. There will be “growing pains,” as Roberts said after Tuesday’s performance. The manager said he “didn’t love” the quality of De Paula’s at-bats. But October is a scenario De Paula feels he will be ready for.
“Especially in big moments, I feel like my mind just goes to a whole ‘nother level,” De Paula said. “Especially competing. The bigger the moment is … it’s like the more my mind hyper-focuses. So when I’m hyper-focused like that a lot, it’s dangerous.”

item.title: [True Blue LA] Dodgers notes: Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Teoscar Hernández, Shohei Ohtani
item.dc:creator: Jacob Macofsky
item.description: The Dodgers’ winning ways in September were briefly interrupted for two games against the Miami Marlins, but they have picked back up against the Cincinnati Reds, taking the first two games of a four-game set. After Tarik Skubal shut down Cincinnati over seven innings on Monday, Yoshinobu Yamamoto continued the trend of marvelous results from the rotation with a seven-inning scoreless gem on Tuesday, working through a pair of lead-off walks while allowing just one hit while striking out seven. Y
item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers’ winning ways in September were briefly interrupted for two games against the Miami Marlins, but they have picked back up against the Cincinnati Reds, taking the first two games of a four-game set.
After Tarik Skubal shut down Cincinnati over seven innings on Monday, Yoshinobu Yamamoto continued the trend of marvelous results from the rotation with a seven-inning scoreless gem on Tuesday, working through a pair of lead-off walks while allowing just one hit while striking out seven. Yamamoto has amazed in his two most recent starts— both against the Reds— allowing just one run over 14 innings while racking up 17 strikeouts compared to just three walks.
Yamamoto held the Reds to just a 1-21 clip after walking his first two hitters of the game on Tuesday, and the right-hander managed to take a page out of Skubal’s playbook for his dominating efforts, notes Sonja Chen of MLB.com.
Yamamoto was able to learn from how the Reds approached Skubal the night before, and Snell was no doubt gathering similar information on Tuesday.
“That kind of encouraged me to be aggressive and attack the hitters,” Yamamoto said through interpreter Yoshihiro Sonoda.
The pitching has managed to hold their end of the bargain against Cincinnati this week, and Blake Snell looks to keep that trajectory in motion. On the offensive side of the ball, Teoscar Hernández has fortified the offense at Great American Ball Park, as the right-hander has crushed a pair of two-run home runs that put both games out of reach.
Hernández has once again found his stride that fans saw during spring training this year, and the Dodger outfielder’s recent success is the brainchild of hitting coach Aaron Bates, allowing Hernández to have a “twister tap” in his stride to the ball, per Maddie Lee of the Los Angeles Times.
“It was a great meeting we had,” Bates said. “We all talked about it, and then he felt comfortable enough to do it, and then the rest is to his credit. He’s just been who he is.”
“When Teo’s hips are loose that way, and his front leg looks like an Elvis knee, it’s a good sign for us,” Bates said. “Because that means that he can open and close it without his upper body going with it.”
Update on Shohei Ohtani
It’s an unusual feeling watching the Dodgers without Shohei Ohtani in the everyday lineup. So far, rookie Josue De Paula has filled in at DH to a small degree of success in limited time (.143/.368/.429, 19 PA) while the reigning two-time NL MVP recovers from multiple nagging issues.
Jack Harris of the California Post notes that Ohtani was able to take batting practice on Monday, and the team is optimistic that he can potentially return from the injured list before the end of the regular season.
“Today was positive,” Roberts said, “and hopefully we can just keep building towards that.”

item.title: [Bleed Cubbie Blue] MLB News: Roberto Clemente Day, Shohei Ohtani, Pete Alonso, Aaron Judge, Arizona Fall League, Gerrit Cole
item.dc:creator: Ashley MacLennan
item.description: Tuesday was Roberto Clemente Day in MLB, celebrating one of the most outstanding humans to ever play baseball, and annually it is used as an opportunity to honor both Latin players and also the humanitarian and charitable efforts of players on every team by nominating a candidate for the season’s Roberto Clemente Award. It’s a good day to remember all the good that Clemente did, but also all the good he continues to inspire. We will also look at some more controversial topics, like whether or no
item.content:encoded:
Tuesday was Roberto Clemente Day in MLB, celebrating one of the most outstanding humans to ever play baseball, and annually it is used as an opportunity to honor both Latin players and also the humanitarian and charitable efforts of players on every team by nominating a candidate for the season’s Roberto Clemente Award. It’s a good day to remember all the good that Clemente did, but also all the good he continues to inspire.
We will also look at some more controversial topics, like whether or not it’s time for the Braves to consider selling the team, or if it’s time for Shohei Ohtani to give up pitching for good. Plus, is Gerrit Cole putting too much blame on the ABS system for his pitching woes?
There’s all that and more below, so let’s get right into it!
- Dan Szymborski wonders if Gavin Williams is a legit ace.
- Arizona Fall League rosters have been revealed. (MLB)
- A look at some other players who have managed to have a 10 WAR season. (MLB)
- Ryan Phillips thinks it’s time that Shohei Ohtani give up pitching for good.
- Evan Drellich explains why one Braves’ investor thinks now is the time to sell the team. (The Athletic subscription required.)
- On Roberto Clemente Day, Jorge Castillo takes a deep dive into the declining numbers of Puerto Rican players in MLB.
- Aaron Judge got his first home run after his return from the IL, and helped the Yankees clinch a postseason berth. (AP)
- Jim Bowden assesses what is and isn’t fair in the CBA negotiations from the perspective of a former exec. (The Athletic subscription required.)
- This is a crazy at-bat.
- David Laurila talks to the delightful Sean Doolittle about pitching.
- Does height really matter? In baseball it sure does, and Davy Andrews explains why.
- With 14 straight, the Dodgers have tied the record for consecutive playoff clinches. Story by Sonja Chen.
- Andy Demetra shares the story of a banned minor leaguer who changed his name to sneak back into the majors.
- Terry Francona seemed relieved by reports that there would be no major changes in the Reds’ front office. (AP)
- Tom Verducci explains why Gerrit Cole can’t blame the ABS for his pitching woes.
- Pete Alonso was touched by the crowd’s welcome in his return to Citi Field. (AP)
- Tyler Kepner bemoans the Mets’ loss of Alonso and their inability to replace him. (The Athletic subscription required.)
- Your 2026 Roberto Clemente Award nominees.
- Jay Jaffe checks in on the Cy Young races and the leading candidates for both leagues.
- Jared Greenspan also checks in on the likely (and possibly unanimous) Cy Young winners.
- Ben Clemens talks to Noah Cameron about how his worst pitch actually made him better.
- Kiri Oler checks in on how the San Francisco Firebells are dominating the WPBL postseason.
- Ian Browne looks at what the return of Garrett Crochet could mean for the Red Sox.
- Karl Rasmussen rounds up some milestones that could be set in the final weeks of the season.
- David Purdum looks at the rising threat of angry bettors as sports betting continues to grow.
- The biggest success and disappointment on each MLB team. Story by Bradford Doolittle.
- Sam Blum revisits Yasiel Puig’s conviction and wonders why he has yet to be sentenced. (The Athletic subscription required.)
- A good reminder on Roberto Clemente Day.
And tomorrow will be a better day than today, Buster. Make it so.

item.title: [cocokara-next.com] 「投手を続ける価値が本当にあるのか…」米誌が大谷翔平に“勧告” 二刀流継続で「度重なる代償を払い続けている」
item.description: 「投手を続ける価値が本当にあるのか…」米誌が大谷翔平に“勧告” 二刀流継続で「度重なる代償を払い続けている」 大谷は二刀流を終える時なのか。米誌が見解を示した(C)Getty Images ドジャースの大谷翔平は二刀流を終える時なのか。右上腕二頭筋と左膝の不調を抱えて負傷者リスト（IL）入りしている大谷について、米誌『Sports Illustrated』の電子版『Dodgers ON SI』が見解を示した。 同誌は「かつてないほどに打席でもマウンドでも圧倒的な存在感を放つオオタニだが、投球を続けることが彼の身体に及ぼしてきた負担を考えれば、投手を続ける価値が本当にあるのかを決断すべき時がきている」と伝えた。 さらに「率直に言って、私たちは2度と彼がピッチャーマウンドに立つ姿を見るべきではないのかもしれない」と、厳しい言葉を投げかけた。 今季の大谷は投手として8勝2敗、防御率1.79、95奪三振の好成績を収めており「球界初の本格的な二刀流スターとなった彼の凄まじい才能を、私たちは改めて見せつけられた。しかし残念ながら、その才能を維持することで、度重なる代償を払い続けている」と主張した。
item.content:encoded:
「投手を続ける価値が本当にあるのか…」米誌が大谷翔平に“勧告” 二刀流継続で「度重なる代償を払い続けている」
大谷は二刀流を終える時なのか。米誌が見解を示した(C)Getty Images
ドジャースの大谷翔平は二刀流を終える時なのか。右上腕二頭筋と左膝の不調を抱えて負傷者リスト（IL）入りしている大谷について、米誌『Sports Illustrated』の電子版『Dodgers ON SI』が見解を示した。
同誌は「かつてないほどに打席でもマウンドでも圧倒的な存在感を放つオオタニだが、投球を続けることが彼の身体に及ぼしてきた負担を考えれば、投手を続ける価値が本当にあるのかを決断すべき時がきている」と伝えた。
さらに「率直に言って、私たちは2度と彼がピッチャーマウンドに立つ姿を見るべきではないのかもしれない」と、厳しい言葉を投げかけた。
今季の大谷は投手として8勝2敗、防御率1.79、95奪三振の好成績を収めており「球界初の本格的な二刀流スターとなった彼の凄まじい才能を、私たちは改めて見せつけられた。しかし残念ながら、その才能を維持することで、度重なる代償を払い続けている」と主張した。
続けて「フルタイムの先発投手と毎試合出場する打者を両立させようとする中で、オオタニは長年にわたり数々のケガに見舞われてきた。これまでの取り組みが打席での能力に影を落とすことはなかったが、32歳となった今、ついにその影響が出始めているように見受けられる」と、二刀流による弊害を指摘した。

item.title: [Los Angeles Times] How Teoscar Hernández fixed his swing to help power Dodgers over the Reds

item.content:encoded:
How Teoscar Hernández fixed his swing to help power Dodgers over the Reds
- Click here to listen to this article
-
CINCINNATI — A simple change opened a dramatic offensive turnaround for Dodgers left fielder Teoscar Hernández.
Hernández’s two-run homer Tuesday, in the Dodgers’ 4-0 win against the Reds, was his second home run in as many nights, as the team trimmed its magic number to clinch the division to one behind Yoshinobu Yamamoto’s seven innings of one-hit ball. And, significantly, this one was against a right-handed pitcher.
“It’s been very helpful,” manager Dave Roberts said after the game. “As certain guys are not seeing the ball as well, it’s nice to kind of backfill with guys like Teo swinging the bat. And when you can slug like he can, you can win baseball games, and he can carry us for a while. And the last 10 days, something like that, it’s been really good from him.”
Through the end of August, Hernández had just a .668 OPS against right-handed pitchers this season. So, when Roberts was asked in Detroit whether the Dodgers would consider setting up a left-field platoon with the team’s September call-ups, he said yes.
Hernández homered off Tigers left-hander Framber Valdez on the last day of the series. And before the Dodgers opened a three-game set against the Cardinals at Dodger Stadium, Hernández met with the hitting coaches.
Against Valdez, Hernández was in a closed stance, to delay his front hip from opening, according to Dodgers hitting coach Aaron Bates. But the team’s hitting group thought a return to a familiar setup could be a long-term solution.
“It was a great meeting we had,” Bates said. “We all talked about it, and then he felt comfortable enough to do it, and then the rest is to his credit. He’s just been who he is.”
Edwin Díaz struggled in his rehab start Sunday, and Dave Roberts is making it clear the Dodgers “got to see something” before putting him on the playoff roster.
In the past, Hernández had used a “twister tap” as his stride. He started in a more open stance, tapped his toe in line with the pitcher, and then set his foot down. But lower-body injuries the last couple of years — a left groin strain last season and a left hamstring strain earlier this season — forced him away from it.
His improved health and hip flexibility opened the avenue for him to return to that timing mechanism.
“When Teo’s hips are loose that way, and his front leg looks like an Elvis knee, it’s a good sign for us,” Bates said. “Because that means that he can open and close it without his upper body going with it.”
The advantage of the twister tap, as Hernández explained it, is how repeatable it is. A more traditional stride can be sped up or slowed down.
“Just being able to control my body and being in a good position,” Hernández said earlier this month. “I can see the pitch a little sooner and identify what kind of pitch it is and if it’s going to be a strike or a ball.”
With that change, he’s rewarded the Dodgers for deciding against platooning left field. Hernández entered Tuesday with a .777 OPS against right-handed pitchers — a sample size of just 28 plate appearances but still a significant jump.
“The biggest thing is his plate coverage away,” Bates said. “Because now he can spoil pitches, and he’s staying in at-bats longer.”
Hernández’s dramatic offensive turnaround, along with fellow corner outfielder Kyle Tucker’s improvement, have helped steady a Dodgers offense that’s missing Shohei Ohtani (on the IL with right biceps and left knee injuries) and includes a hobbled Freddie Freeman (right knee soreness).
Rookie Josue De Paula, mostly filling in for Ohtani at designated hitter, has already shown he can take mature at-bats and provide some pop. But he’s still finding his footing in a new league.
It lengthens the Dodgers lineup for Hernández, after a slow start to his year, to return to being a veteran power threat — just in time to, ideally, carry the momentum into the postseason.
On Monday, he launched his two-run shot off left-hander Nick Lodolo. On Tuesday, he replicated the feat off right-hander Rhett Lowder.
On the second pitch of the at-bat, Hernández recognized a hung slider, and he roped it over the left-field fence at 109.3 mph, according to Statcast. The blast put the Dodgers up 3-0 in the third inning, with Dodgers starter Yamamoto settling into a groove on the other side.
Yamamoto had walked the first two batters he faced, but he reined in his control to pitch seven scoreless innings and allow just one more baserunner — a double by Reds star shortstop Elly De La Cruz.
The Dodgers also scored on Hunter Feduccia’s second-inning single and Alex Freeland’s seventh-inning homer. And the Dodgers bullpen completed the shutout.
Freeman staying in the lineup
Freeman was all smiles after his three-hit game Tuesday — after going hitless for his last four games.
“I was supposed to be off tomorrow, but I played myself in there,” he said. “So I’m very excited.”
Roberts explained: “He was joking, saying, ‘If I get three hits, then can I be in there tomorrow?’”
Sure enough, the mechanical adjustments he made in the batting cage — focusing on getting his foot down early and making contact out in front — got him there.
“I’m just trying to find something that gives me results,” Freeman said. “We’re at the time where we’re just trying to get hot for five weeks here. So kind of like I did in the World Series a couple years ago, I did the step-out move. That’s not sustainable over six months. I’m not trying to find something that’s sustainable.”
Though Roberts has been trying to find opportunities to rest Freeman, he saw promising signs Tuesday beyond the results.
“Just my eyes, just watching him move, I feel good about him going tomorrow,” Roberts said.
De Paula, Freeland and third baseman Max Muncy will be out of the lineup Wednesday, Roberts said.

item.title: [sports.yahoo.com] Yoshinobu Yamamoto's 4-pitch leadoff walk was a red flag, but the Dodgers' ace proved it was a fluke
item.dc:creator: Jake Mintz

item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI — Before each start, Yoshinobu Yamamoto does something remarkable.
Many pitchers long toss as part of their pregame routine. It's common practice at the high school level and above to warm up the arm, boot up the body, rev up the engine. Throwing a ball far is mighty similar, biomechanically, to throwing a ball fast.
But Yamamoto takes things to another level. After subjecting his muscles and ligaments to an elaborate stretching program, the Dodgers righty begins playing catch, gradually working his way toward the outer reaches of a big-league park's center-field grasslands. First 200 feet, then 250, 275, up to around 300. But instead of winding himself up with a few hop-steps like most long-tossers do, Yamamoto lets it fly from the relative standstill of his usual in-game windup.
It's a mesmerizing thing to witness — this 5-foot-10, 176-pound speck of cerulean catapulting a baseball 100 yards without the help of any real momentum. For a few seconds after release, Yamamoto stands frozen, balancing on his left leg with his right leg dangling in the air. The whole thing looks fake, like a lazy AI generation. How could a dude that small throw a ball that far that easily?
Such is the magic of Yamamoto: balance, intention, mechanical precision.
All those qualities and more were on display Tuesday in Cincinnati as the undersized hurler tore the Reds asunder. He worked seven scoreless innings, struck out seven and allowed just one hit.
After walking the first two hitters of the game, Yamamoto settled in. Following Elly De La Cruz's double in the third, the Dodgers starter retired the final 13 hitters he faced.
"He's able to reset on the fly. He's able to bear down and make pitches when he needs to," manager Dave Roberts explained after L.A.'s 4-0 win.
Yamamoto needed that adjustability Tuesday after an uncharacteristically poor start to the outing. He walked Cincinnati leadoff man Carlos Jorge, making just the fifth start of his MLB career, on four wayward offerings. It was the first time in Yamamoto's stateside tenure that he walked the first batter of the game on four pitches. He was similarly over-careful with the following hitter, walking De La Cruz on a 3-1 count. Jorge reached third base on a sac fly but got no further, as Yamamoto escaped the frame with no damage.
"At the beginning, because I [didn't] have my usual stuff mechanically, so mentally I was very calm, and then still kept composed, so I was able to make an adjustment on time," Yamamoto said afterward.
From there, it was business as usual, with Yamamoto deploying his typical barrage of splitters, curves and heaters. It was metronomical, almost humdrum, the way Yamamoto eased through the outing with little trouble. You blinked, and he was in the seventh with a zero on the board.
His entire season has carried a similar energy. The National League's overabundance of headline hurlers has been one of this campaign's main storylines. Jacob Misiorowski looks primed to win his first Cy Young behind a historic, bat-missing stat line. Chris Sale, Cristopher Sánchez, Jesús Luzardo and Chase Burns have all been excellent as well. Those characters, to a certain extent, have overshadowed Yamamoto's contributions.
This tumultuous Dodgers season, too, has stolen some of the shine. So much attention has been paid to the health and exploits of Shohei Ohtani and his quest to reestablish himself as a two-way dynamo over a full season. L.A.'s acquisition of Tarik Skubal overtook the trade deadline. Through it all, Yamamoto has remained magnificently consistent.
And with October just around the corner, the 2025 World Series hero is looking primed to carry the torch for the Dodgers once again.

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers finally get positive injury updates on Shohei Ohtani, Freddie Freeman
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris
item.description: CINCINNATI — For the first time in what’s felt like a while, the Dodgers’ usually foreboding daily injury updates came with some needed signs of optimism on Tuesday. Before the game, manager Dave Roberts said two-way star Shohei Ohtani “felt good” after resuming hitting activities on Monday, when he took swings off a tee back in Los Angeles. And while Roberts didn’t guarantee Ohtani would return from the injured list before the end of the regular season, that at least remains the team’s expectat
item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI — For the first time in what’s felt like a while, the Dodgers’ usually foreboding daily injury updates came with some needed signs of optimism on Tuesday.
Before the game, manager Dave Roberts said two-way star Shohei Ohtani “felt good” after resuming hitting activities on Monday, when he took swings off a tee back in Los Angeles. And while Roberts didn’t guarantee Ohtani would return from the injured list before the end of the regular season, that at least remains the team’s expectation for now.
“Today was positive,” Roberts said, “and hopefully we can just keep building towards that.”
Then, in an even bigger development, first baseman Freddie Freeman not only returned to the lineup in Tuesday night’s win over the Cincinnati Reds, but put together a three-hit performance that “played myself in” to Wednesday’s lineup, he proudly noted with a grin.
Initially, Roberts was planning to rest Freeman on Wednesday amid his ongoing battle with a right knee injury. That would have marked the 37-year-old’s fourth missed game out of the last seven for the team.
Early in the night, however, Freeman struck a deal with his manager.
“He was joking, saying, ‘If I get three hits, then can I be in there tomorrow?’” Roberts recounted.
Right on cue, Freeman lined singles in the first, fifth and seventh innings — snapping out of his troubling 3-for-30 slump previously.
“It looked good,” Roberts said. “It looked more like Freddie.”
Not only did the veteran slugger feel no pain in his knee — where he has been battling a patellar tendinitis problem — but he also revealed a fruitful adjustment he had made before the game with his swing.
Amid his recent knee problems, Freeman felt he had started letting the ball travel too far in his stance before beginning his swing, causing him to “slide” in the box, especially with a compromised front leg.
Thus, he made a temporary change he hopes will spark him ahead of the playoffs, focusing on getting his front leg down sooner and catching the ball further out at the front of his swing.
“I feel like my faults are I try to hit the ball to the opposite field too much, and I let the ball get too deep,” he said. “So today was [get the] foot down early, catch the ball out front a little bit, and it kind of worked. I wasn’t squaring the ball up in the game, but I’ll take those three hits and keep that work going tomorrow, and hopefully we’ll get hot.”
It’s not a permanent solution, Freeman noted. But at this point in the year, “I’m not trying to find something that’s sustainable,” he said. “I’m trying to find something that works for four weeks.”
Indeed, between that and Ohtani’s progress — which has the Dodgers remaining cautiously optimistic about his chances to make an impact in the playoffs — it was enough for the team to finally feel some optimism about the way they are trending toward October, getting a couple of positive updates on two of their superstar hitters.

item.content:encoded:
How did Josue De Paula do for Dodgers vs. Reds on Sept. 15?
Josue De Paula made his first start as the Los Angeles Dodgers' leadoff hitter on Tuesday, Sept. 15.
He went 0-for-5 at the plate in the Dodgers' 4-0 win over the Cincinnati Reds.
The 21-year-old designated hitter jumped up into the leadoff spot in place of Tommy Edman, who was originally in the role after Shohei Ohtani's injury woes.
De Paula added to the Dodgers' offense in a game against the Miami Marlins, hitting a three-run home run for his first career homer on Sept. 13.
The 21-year-old De Paula made his major-league debut for the team at LoanDepot Park on Friday, Sept. 11, becoming the youngest Dodgers player since Alex Verdugo on Sept. 2, 2017.
De Paula has been viewed as the organization's top prospect and recently became the first Dodgers position player called up from AA, while skipping AAA, since Steve Sax in 1981.

item.description: アパレルブランド「BOSS」の公式インスタグラムが16日までに更新され、米大リーグ、ドジャースの大谷翔平投手（32）が登場した。 「BOSS」の公式インスタには「BOSS」の秋の新作に身を包んだ大谷が登場。シックなデザインの秋らしい装いの写真を複数アップし「洗練されたBOSSの最新スタイルに身を包んだ大谷翔平から秋の装いを見直そう」と呼びかけた。 また大谷が出演する動画も公開され、ボールやバットを手に力強い視線を投げかけており、「あなたの考え方、あなたの力、あなたのスタイルを見せて」とつづっている。 この他にもインスタには、陸上女子の中距離走で活躍するアリカ・シュミット（27）＝ドイツ＝や、自動車F1のドライバー、フェルナンド・アロンソ（45）＝スペイン＝、NFLの若手スターQBジャクソン・ダート（23）＝米国＝が登場しており、世界のスーパースターの豪華共演となっている。 大谷は「右上腕二頭筋の炎症」で負傷者リスト（IL）入りしており、15日から打撃活動を再開。IL明けは23日（同24日）となっている。実戦復帰までこなす過程は多く、レギュラーシーズン中の復帰は不透明となっている。

アパレルブランド「BOSS」の公式インスタグラムが16日までに更新され、米大リーグ、ドジャースの大谷翔平投手（32）が登場した。
「BOSS」の公式インスタには「BOSS」の秋の新作に身を包んだ大谷が登場。シックなデザインの秋らしい装いの写真を複数アップし「洗練されたBOSSの最新スタイルに身を包んだ大谷翔平から秋の装いを見直そう」と呼びかけた。
また大谷が出演する動画も公開され、ボールやバットを手に力強い視線を投げかけており、「あなたの考え方、あなたの力、あなたのスタイルを見せて」とつづっている。
この他にもインスタには、陸上女子の中距離走で活躍するアリカ・シュミット（27）＝ドイツ＝や、自動車F1のドライバー、フェルナンド・アロンソ（45）＝スペイン＝、NFLの若手スターQBジャクソン・ダート（23）＝米国＝が登場しており、世界のスーパースターの豪華共演となっている。
大谷は「右上腕二頭筋の炎症」で負傷者リスト（IL）入りしており、15日から打撃活動を再開。IL明けは23日（同24日）となっている。実戦復帰までこなす過程は多く、レギュラーシーズン中の復帰は不透明となっている。

item.title: [New York Post] Yoshinobu Yamamoto rounds into playoff form as Dodgers move to cusp of NL West title
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris
item.description: CINCINNATI –– There’s not much the Dodgers can do, manager Dave Roberts said Tuesday afternoon, to get their all-important rotation ready for the added workload that will come in the postseason. item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI –– There’s not much the Dodgers can do, manager Dave Roberts said Tuesday afternoon, to get their all-important rotation ready for the added workload that will come in the postseason.
Over the final couple weeks of the regular season, they have to just keep running their starters out there, and counting on them to round into elevated October form.
That’s what appeared to happen with Yoshinobu Yamamoto on Tuesday night at Great American Ball Park, in what was the right-hander’s most dominant performance of at least the last couple months.
In the Dodgers’ 4-0 win over the Cincinnati Reds, Yamamoto threw a one-hit masterpiece over seven scoreless innings, flashing the kind of ruthless efficiency that defined his heroics during last year’s playoffs.
After walking his first two batters in the first inning, he retired 21 of the 22 after with seven strikeouts and virtually no stress.
“After the first two hitters, it was vintage Yama,” Roberts said. “Just attacking, not trying to be too fine.”
The reigning World Series MVP hadn’t exactly been struggling lately, of course. Just last week, he held the Reds to one run over seven innings with 10 strikeouts back in Los Angeles.
But what Yamamoto did on Tuesday was different, keyed by quick and easy outs on soft and harmless contact.
It’s what he did as the ace of last year’s postseason staff, and what he will need to do again as the Dodgers go for a World Series three-peat this fall.
“I’d like to carry this,” Yamamoto said through an interpreter of his renewed stuff, “into October.”
The Dodgers are hoping they won’t have to ask as much out of Yamamoto this time around; that they need him to pitch back-to-back complete games (like he did in Game 2 of the NLCS and Game 2 of the World Series) or provide back-to-back nights of season-saving heroics (following up a victorious Game 6 start in the Fall Classic with a winning three-inning appearance out of the bullpen in Game 7).
But in a postseason environment, it’s impossible to know what exactly will be required.
“You can’t just try to create that during the regular season because you want these guys as strong and healthy for the October run [as possible],” Roberts said pregame. “But it’s one of those things that, once we get to the postseason, all bets are off and everyone is going to do what they can to contribute.”
It would help, of course, if the Dodgers’ currently Shohei Ohtani-less offense can keep turning a corner, with Tuesday bringing more positive –– albeit subtle –– signs.
The biggest development: Freddie Freeman returned to the lineup amid his ongoing right knee injury, and finally snapped out of a 3-for-30 slump by collecting three singles in the first, fifth and seventh innings.
“Feels better today than he did yesterday,” Roberts said, after Freeman missed his third game in the last week on Monday, “which is a good thing.”
The Dodgers’ scoring, meanwhile, came from elsewhere.

Hunter Feduccia laced an RBI single in the second off Reds starter Rhett Lowder, maintaining his unexpected status as the Dodgers’ best hitter against right-handed pitching since being re-acquired at the trade deadline (with a team-leading .292 average in such splits since the start of August).
Teoscar Hernández continued his late-season surge with a two-run homer in the third, giving him four home runs, eight extra-base hits, 18 RBIs and a .417 average over his last 14 games.
Even Alex Freeland chipped in with a solo blast in the seventh and a double in the ninth, helping him outshine fellow rookie Josue De Paula (who went 0-for-5 with his first two strikeouts of the season after getting bumped up to the leadoff spot).
That was all enough to help the team lower its magic number to clinch the National League West to one.
Still, when it comes to October, no position group will be more important than the Dodgers’ rotation.
That’s why, right now, outings like the one Yamamoto made on Tuesday, or Tarik Skubal spun the night before (also seven scoreless innings) are the most promising ways the Dodgers can ramp up toward the playoffs.
Once they get there, they’ll need their starters to be on.

item.content:encoded:
Dodgers news: Shohei Ohtani, Andy Pages get big injury updates before playoffs appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
With a spot in the MLB playoff locked up, the Los Angeles Dodgers have one major goal for the rest of September: get healthy.
Sure, there are sub-storylines to follow, from Josue De Paula filling in at DH, which bullpen arms are getting hot at the right time, and Kyle Tucker figuring it out down the stretch, but for the most part, the Dodgers simply want to take the field in October with their best guys all available for Dave Roberts to call upon.
Fortunately, on Tuesday, Roberts provided fans with some positive updates on that very front, noting that Shohei Ohtani and Andy Pages are trending in the right direction, as reported by The Athletic's Fabian Ardaya.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
"Some more from Dave Roberts: Shohei Ohtani hit in the cage today. Hope is still for him to return before the end of the regular season," Ardaya wrote. "Andy Pages hit off the machine today. Plan is for him to do Trajekt next. Bullpen game on Thursday."
After breaking his hand in mid-August in a game against the Pittsburgh Pirates, Pages has missed almost a month as he works back from surgery. And as for Ohtani? Well, after missing four games earlier in the month, he returned for one but didn't ultimately look right, landing on the IL to allow him to recover from a series of injuries that have hampered his production down the stretch.
Without Pages and Ohtani, the Dodgers still found a way to manufacture offense, ripping off their longest win streak of the season, but folding that duo back into the fray, especially with De Paula proving he deserves a spot on the bench as a power-hitting pinch hitter, makes LA all the more dangerous down the stretch.
Related: Bobby Miller gets brutally honest on returning to Dodgers
Related: Why Dodgers' Dave Roberts is leading off Josue De Paula vs. Reds

item.title: [MLB.com] Ohtani begins hitting progression, as regular-season return remains in sight
item.dc:creator: Sonja Chen

item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI -- Shohei Ohtani resumed swinging on Tuesday for the first time since landing on the 15-day injured list last week, manager Dave Roberts said before the Dodgers' game against the Reds at Great American Ball Park.
Ohtani is not on the road with the Dodgers, but he hit off a tee in L.A. and came away feeling good afterward, Roberts said. It was Ohtani's first time swinging since his lingering right biceps and left knee injuries led him to be shut down starting last Wednesday.
"I don't know what's in store for tomorrow, but I know that there's going to be a consistent buildup," Roberts said. "Don't know when the time of return to play is, but today was positive, and hopefully we can just keep building towards that."
Ohtani's 15-day IL placement is backdated to Sept. 8, meaning that the earliest he can be activated is Sept. 23, with five regular-season games remaining for the Dodgers. Roberts believes that Ohtani will be back in action before the end of the regular season.
"Whether it happens or not is to be determined, but I do expect him to be back to play in some regular-season games," Roberts said. "Don't know how many of them."
In his last 24 games, a span that coincided with an attempt to ramp up as a pitcher, Ohtani hit .198 (19-for-96) with a .690 OPS and 34 strikeouts. Toward the end of that stretch, he began to look physically compromised at the plate, leading the Dodgers to leave him out of the lineup for four straight games. He returned to the lineup on Sept. 7 but did not come away from that game feeling good.
At that point, the Dodgers opted to place Ohtani on the IL with the aim of getting him right for the postseason. He will return only as a hitter, with his two-way duties shelved until 2027.
The Dodgers have fared well without their best hitter, entering Tuesday having won nine of the 11 games they played since Ohtani was first held out of the lineup on Sept. 3. They clinched their record-tying 14th consecutive postseason berth on Monday and are close to winning their 13th NL West title in that span, all while remaining in position to secure a first-round bye.
The understanding is that Ohtani will probably not feel 100 percent in the postseason, but he'll use the weeks ahead to feel as good as he can, both physically and with his swing. While the Dodgers have gotten by without him, they know they'll need whatever they can get from him as they bid for a three-peat.

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers rookie Josue De Paula may be known for his big bat, but it's the times he doesn't swing that are drawing comparisons to a future Hall of Famer.
De Paula has only two hits in his young MLB career — granted, one of them was a huge home run — but he's walked five times, recording at least one in each of his four games, without even a single strikeout.
That kind of plate discipline — and De Paula's funny reaction to pitches outside of the strike zone — have an unexpected superstar showing love to the young Dodger.
Rival player supports Josue De Paula
New York Met Juan Soto, who's battled the Dodgers as a member of the San Diego Padres and New York Yankees, took to Instagram to shout out his fellow Dominican slugger.
Sharing MLB's video of De Paula shaking his head at a pitch below his knees in a moment reminiscent of the "Soto shuffle," Soto gassed up the young slugger.
In Spanish, Soto praised De Paula, whom he called "my crazy friend," for "staying locked in at the plate."
As Dodgers Nation's Noel Sanchez pointed out, the two truly are friends, and their shared history goes beyond just the ability to take a walk or hit a home run.
"These two both attended El Niche Baseball Academy early in their respective careers and they've trained together in the past," Sanchez said. "In a sports world where comparison can be the thief of joy, it's so nice to see Soto co-signing De Paula after his early success."
Of course, Dodgers faithful probably aren't huge fans of Soto.
He and the Padres knocked the Dodgers out of the playoffs in 2022, and he spurned the Boys in Blue to sign with the Mets on a contract even bigger than that of superstar Shohei Ohtani.
That said, Soto's ability to recognize the talents of a younger player — even on another NL team — is worth celebrating, Sanchez said.
"A lot of Dodger fans don't show him love but like I said, everyone should respect this," he said.
What do you think of Juan Soto showing love to Josue De Paula?

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Dodgers' Dave Roberts Sent Kyle Tucker Clear Message in One-on-One Meeting
item.dc:creator: J P Hoornstra; Unknown
item.description: Kyle Tucker's home run Monday in Cincinnati was his third in his last five games. In that span he's raised his slugging percentage from a season-low .350 on Sept. 8 to .376 entering Tuesday's rematch against the Reds. September is halfway through, and it's shaping into Tucker's best month of the season. If it seems like he's stopped pressing at the plate, perhaps Tucker let up on himself after getting some needed reassurance in a one-on-one meeting with Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts.
item.content:encoded:
Kyle Tucker's home run Monday in Cincinnati was his third in his last five games. In that span he's raised his slugging percentage from a season-low .350 on Sept. 8 to .376 entering Tuesday's rematch against the Reds.
September is halfway through, and it's shaping into Tucker's best month of the season. If it seems like he's stopped pressing at the plate, perhaps Tucker let up on himself after getting some needed reassurance in a one-on-one meeting with Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts.
“I told him, I’m gonna ride or die with him,” Roberts said (via Jack Harris of the California Post). “That was my young term phrase.”
It's been a rough ride for Tucker in his first season in Los Angeles. The Dodgers signed the four-time All-Star to a four-year, $240 million contract over the winter. Despite being baseball's highest-paid player this season, Tucker hit only one home run in his first 17 games of the season.
Things didn't get much better from there. Among 138 qualified hitters through the end of August, Tucker's .683 OPS ranked 116th.
"I was prepared, the organization was prepared, to give him as much leash as we possibly could to work through some things, and I do think that now we’re starting to see the fruits,” Roberts said. “So I see no other reason why we would pivot from running him out there every day.”
Fans might beg to differ.
At Triple-A Oklahoma City, outfielder James Tibbs III has 29 home runs and 101 RBIs to go with a .417 on-base percentage. Prospect Josue De Paula, who's played right field in the minors, was promoted to take Shohei Ohtani's place on the active roster.
Since his debut, the 21-year-old has reached base in half of his first 14 plate appearances. Sunday, he hit his first career home run. Perhaps Roberts needed to reassure Tucker that De Paula wasn't coming for his job to unlock his production, a curious case of reverse psychology.
It will be hard for the Dodgers to take De Paula out of the lineup if he maintains his current level of production. Roberts said prior to Ohtani's IL stint that the team wasn't considering using him in the outfield.
Tucker, for his part, can reduce the Dodgers' temptation to use Ohtani or De Paula in right field if he continues to hit like a $60 million All-Star.

J.P. Hoornstra is an On SI Contributor. A veteran of 20 years of sports coverage for daily newspapers in California, J.P. covered MLB, the Los Angeles Dodgers, and the Los Angeles Angels (occasionally of Anaheim) from 2012-23 for the Southern California News Group. His first book, The 50 Greatest Dodgers Games of All-Time, published in 2015. In 2016, he won an Associated Press Sports Editors award for breaking news coverage. He once recorded a keyboard solo on the same album as two of the original Doors.

And yet, that wasn’t the biggest surprise in the team’s new-look batting order. item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI –– Despite Freddie Freeman’s ongoing right knee injury, the veteran first baseman was back in the Dodgers’ lineup on Tuesday.
And yet, that wasn’t the biggest surprise in the team’s new-look batting order.
Instead, rookie designated hitter Josue De Paula got an auspicious bump up for the club, getting the chance to serve as leadoff hitter for Tuesday’s matchup against Reds right-hander Rhett Lowder.
Tuesday only marked De Paula’s fifth game in the majors, following his call-up directly from double-A Tulsa last week.
He is still serving as DH on only a temporary basis, with Shohei Ohtani on the injured list nursing left knee and right arm injuries.
However, the 21-year-old top prospect has already made a positive impression, drawing five walks in his first 14 plate appearances while collecting his first two MLB hits on Sunday in Miami with a home run and a double. He is suddenly vying for a potential role in the postseason plans, as well.
Thus, the Dodgers are giving the promising left-handed hitter another new opportunity now, seeing how he looks as the leadoff man in their batting order –– one that was also vacated once Ohtani went on the IL.
“I like the at-bats. I like the at-bat quality,” manager Dave Roberts said. “I understand it’s a small sample, but that’s kind of who he is as a hitter. For me, it’ll be a good opportunity for him to get five at-bats tonight.”
For Freeman, meanwhile, Tuesday marks an important opportunity in its own right, as he tries to show progress with his right knee injury.
Freeman has been out for three of the Dodgers’ last five games because of the ailment, and only DH’d in the game before that.
Since the start of September, he has gone only 3-for-30 at the plate.
Roberts continues to insist an injured list stint won’t be needed for the newly-turned 37-year-old. Both he and Freeman voiced hopes of the injury being resolved (or, at least, not as much of an impediment) by the time the playoffs begin.
“I don’t see him getting to his front side as much as he normally does, which causes him to get a little bit underneath,” Roberts said. “So I know that the hitting guys are on it. He’s working through it, so we’ll see how he comes in today.”
Until he starts to hit again, however, concerns over his health will linger.
On Tuesday, he is batting directly after De Paula in the No. 2 hole.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are in familiar territory with the playoffs less than two weeks away. They are once again looking for answers in their bullpen. The Dodgers have placed Edgardo Henriquez on the IL with lower back discomfort, and he has been ruled out for the remainder of the regular season.
Henriquez has been placed on the 15-day IL, but there remains a path for him returning during the playoffs if all goes well. While the Dodgers made Edwin Diaz a priority this past offseason, it has been Henriquez who has kept the bullpen together.
Through 61 appearances, Henriquez had a 2.85 ERA while striking out over 29% of the hitters he's faced. If he's unable to return to LA's bullpen during the playoffs, the unit is suddenly facing a problem.
Edgardo Henriquez injury leaves Dodgers facing reality they desperately wanted to avoid
While the Dodgers have a healthy amount of left-handed options in the bullpen — considering Tanner Scott once again becoming an effective option at the end of games — as well as Alex Vesia and Jack Dreyer, they don't really have an established option among righties.
Brock Stewart hasn't looked bad this season, but injuries have limited him to just 22 innings pitched this season. Evan Phillips is back in the bullpen, and while he has 3.68 ERA through 27 appearances, his FIP of 4.65 makes him a regression candidate ahead of the playoffs.
It also doesn't help matters that the Dodgers aren't viewing the return of Diaz as a potential solution. He is currently on a minor-league rehab assignment, but the results simply haven't been there. It's forced Dave Roberts to offer a blunt assessment on Diaz earlier this week, suggesting there's a chance he's left off the playoff roster if he can't overcome his current struggles.
That is why Henriquez's injury is such a blow. He was a clear answer for what the Dodgers lacked in the bullpen, and coupling that with Diaz's struggles, Roberts and Co. are back at the drawing board. Perhaps Kris Bubic could be an answer. Bubic is with the Dodgers after a successful rehab assignment earlier this month and is expected to be reinstated from the IL in the coming days.
If there is a silver lining for the Dodgers, outside of Shohei Ohtani, their starting rotation is healthy and that could ultimately prove to be the difference-maker during the playoffs.

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers star first baseman Freddie Freeman does not look like himself right now.
Freeman, who is hitting .293 this season with 16 home runs and an OPS of .818, is dealing with right knee tendinitis.
Since the start of August, the 10-time All-Star is hitting .252 with just one home run and an OPS of .651
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts touched on the injury this past weekend and said that while Freeman is feeling fine enough to play, he's far from the player the team is accustomed to seeing.
“Just talking to him today, he said he felt good,” Roberts said on Sunday, before adding: “Obviously, the swings don’t indicate that, don’t kind of validate that … The last week, it’s pretty obvious that he’s not himself in the box.”
Freeman's knee issue compromises his front side during swings, which has caused extra swing-and-miss at the plate and limited his mobility on defense.
On Monday for the team's series opener against the Cincinnati Reds, Freeman was out of the lineup for the fourth time in the last week.
Roberts said Freeman's injury is one they'll have to manage for the rest of the season.
“I think it’s one of those things where we’ve got to manage it … just pick spots to give him an off day here or there,” Roberts said. “Again, we’ve just got to make sure he’s at optimal health when we finish the season. So I think that he might not love it, but giving him a day off here or there might be beneficial.”
Freeman is expected to avoid an IL stint and remains day-to-day. It remains to be seen if he's back on Tuesday.
"I just think right now, with where we’re at in the season, an IL is not an option in the sense of — I personally don’t think we have a better option," Roberts said. "I don’t think it needs to be 10 days. But could it be more than one? That’s a fair question."
Shohei Ohtani Working His Way Back From Injury
Freeman's injury is just another in a long list of injuries that the Dodgers are dealing with as the regular season winds down.
Freeman is not the only All-SAtar missing time, as Shohei Ohtani is far from healthy as the season winds down.
Ohtani is currently on the 15-day IL with knee, biceps and neck injuries. Roberts said that Ohtani will hit off a tee on Tuesday as he begins his ramp-up.
The 32-year-old is looking to quickly get back as he is eligible to return to the lineup on Sept. 23, just five days before the end of the regular season.
In the meantime, the Dodgers' top prospect, Josue De Paula, has replaced Ohtani as the everyday designated hitter.
If the Dodgers want any chance of completing the three-peat, though, Freeman and Ohtani will need to be healthy and producing at their usual levels.
Thus, the Dodgers will look to get them as close to 100% as possible over the next two weeks.

Ricardo Sandoval is a freelance writer with On SI. He is a graduate of California State University, Northridge, and specializes in sports writing, particularly in MLB, NBA and NFL. He previously served as an Associate Editor for Dodgers Nation and has worked with Newsweek and The Sporting News.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers shortstop Mookie Betts is producing a new movie. On Monday, he announced the project away from the field. He's producing a movie titled "Cannon Street All-Stars."
Los Angeles clinched a playoff berth the same day, beating the Cincinnati Reds 4-1. The win pushed them to 91-59 with 12 games left. It marks the Dodgers' 14th straight postseason appearance.
However, Betts did little to contribute to that win. He went 0-for-4. No hits, home runs or RBIs.
He is having a down year by his standards.
Betts is batting .248 with 20 home runs, 62 RBIs and 108 hits this season. His career average sits at .288. Betts won AL MVP in 2018 and has made eight All-Star teams.
Off the diamond, however, he is excelling in his projects.
More on Mookie Betts' Latest Project
Betts is producing the film alongside Golden State Warriors star Stephen Curry, Deadline reported in an exclusive Monday.
Director Reggie Rock Bythewood and his wife, Gina Prince-Bythewood, are developing the project through their company, Undisputed Cinema. Bythewood will write and direct.
The film tells the true story of the Cannon Street YMCA All-Stars. The all-Black Little League team from Charleston, South Carolina, tried to enter the 1955 state tournament.
Little League baseball in the South remained segregated at the time, eight years after Jackie Robinson broke MLB's color line. The team's push sparked forfeits and national attention. The Jackie Robinson Foundation backs the project.
Bythewood called the film overdue recognition. Surviving players were honored at last year's Little League World Series. "Now it is time to honor them on film," Bythewood said.
Betts produces through his company, OMG Entertainment, alongside Cam Lewis and Omar Bradford. Curry produces through Unanimous Media with Sharla Sumpter Bridgett. Debra Martin Chase and E. Monique Floyd also produce.
Shohei Ohtani, Freddie Freeman Latest Updates
Despite clinching the postseason, few key pieces remain uncertain.
Shohei Ohtani is on the 15-day injured list with left knee and right biceps issues. He landed there Sept. 11.
Manager Dave Roberts said Monday that Ohtani could begin swinging off a tee as early as this week. The Dodgers expect Ohtani back as a hitter in late September. He won't pitch again this season. Ohtani is batting .277 with 30 home runs and 80 RBIs this year.
Freddie Freeman sat out Monday's game to rest a sore right knee, described as patellar tendinitis. The team does not plan to place him on the injured list. Freeman is expected back in the lineup Tuesday.

item.content:encoded:
Dodgers celebran 14to pase seguido a los playoffs con discreto brindis e igualan récord
CINCINNATI — Los Dodgers de Los Ángeles celebraron su 14ta clasificación consecutiva a la postemporada de las Grandes Ligas, para igualar un récord, con un brindis de champán tras la victoria del lunes por la noche por 4-1 sobre los Rojos de Cincinnati.
Las celebraciones más grandes llegarán después.
“Es difícil decir que alguna vez se sienta rutinario, pero esa es la expectativa aquí. Siempre me río cuando aseguramos un lugar en la postemporada: simplemente hacemos un brindis pequeño y agradable”, dijo el tercera base Max Muncy. “Los muchachos que no han estado aquí ven eso y esperan un poco más. Eso pasa cuando aseguras la división”.
Los bicampeones defensores de la Serie Mundial, que se unieron a Milwaukee y Tampa Bay como equipos que ya aseguraron un lugar en los playoffs, redujeron su número mágico a tres para un quinto título consecutivo del Oeste de la Liga Nacional y el 13ro en 14 temporadas.
Los Ángeles igualó la racha de postemporadas de los Bravos de Atlanta de 1991 a 2005. Los Bravos alcanzaron cinco veces a la Serie Mundial durante ese lapso, pero la única vez que se consagraron fue en 1995.
“Por suerte lo estamos haciendo un poco mejor que eso”, dijo Muncy sobre los tres títulos de los Dodgers y sus cinco participaciones en el Clásico de Otoño durante esta racha.
Tarik Skubal —quien lanzó siete entradas sin permitir carreras y concedió apenas tres hits— señaló que la manera en que los Dodgers manejaron el hecho de asegurar un lugar en la postemporada fue definitivamente distinta en comparación con las situaciones de clasificación que vivió las dos temporadas anteriores con Detroit.
“Creo que eso habla de la gente que está en este vestuario y de lo que esperan de este equipo. Eso estuvo genial. Un pequeño brindis y a seguir. Olvidar que pasó. Tenemos más por lograr esta temporada”, expresó.
Dave Roberts, quien cumple su 11ma temporada como mánager, dijo que su mensaje durante el brindis fue que los Dodgers han logrado mucho hasta este punto, pero aún no se han acercado a jugar su mejor béisbol.
“Cada año pasan muchos jugadores por aquí, y los muchachos encuentran la manera de dar un paso al frente, y eso es de lo que probablemente me siento más orgulloso: la consistencia de ganar a largo plazo. Cualquier equipo, cualquier organización puede ganar en un año determinado cuando las cosas se alinean, pero hacerlo todos los años, cuando se espera que lo hagas, dice algo sobre toda la organización”, dijo Roberts.
Los Dodgers (91-59) actualmente son el segundo sembrado en la Liga Nacional. Están dos juegos y medio por delante de Atlanta y están dos juegos detrás de Milwaukee por el primer puesto.
Un pase directo en la primera ronda es importante en cualquier momento, pero especialmente este año para los Dodgers, que no están a plena capacidad. El primera base Freddie Freeman arrastra molestias en la rodilla derecha y Shohei Ohtani, dos veces Jugador Más Valioso de la Liga Nacional, está en la lista de lesionados de 15 días debido a una inflamación en el bíceps derecho.
“Dado cómo están nuestros muchachos en términos de salud, conseguir esa semana sería enorme. Aun así, tenemos que jugar bien para cerrar la temporada y llegar a ese punto”, dijo Roberts antes del juego del lunes.
___

item.title: [Field Level Media] Dodgers' Tarik Skubal looks to duplicate recent outing vs. Reds
item.description: The two-time reigning World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers are closing in on the National League West title and still have their sights on the NL’s top seed.
